items.title: Louis Tio Interview, 1960-10-26
items.q: charlonee and papaya um made a lot of uh music together they played a lot together played a lot of concerts together... charlonee was a very good friend even charlonee was a very good friend in better words charlonee and papaya

ctx.x: Do you remember any special exercises that your brother did or anything? When he practiced, did he ever practiced much at home in late days? Or after he learned to play, did he just play on the job and that was about all? Well, I remember when...

One year before you went to Chicago, my uncle Papaya came to him and told him, he said, You're going amongst some great, great musicians. And he said, when you leave here, don't let nobody food. He said, I know you've been a jazz player all your life, so you can play jazz. But you're going to meet some men that really do know music. And he said, you might confront with that. And sure enough, that's what he did. He got on in the room by himself. He didn't ask nobody for nothing. He just came in there and locked…

That's something to laugh at. That's the truth. And his clarinet, his belt, he had it in his coat pocket, and his two parts of his clarinet wrapped in those steps. Well, you know what kind of impression that must have made on that bandmaster? Yeah, it was funny. What kind of clarinet play out like that? Yeah! You understand? And he told me that there stuck a piece of music, one of the hardest things that he ever read in his life, played in his life. And he came out there and he played that thing with that B-flat…
